newsitem.title: POLAND: EU's Brittan sees progress on Poland disputes.
newsitem.headline: EU's Brittan sees progress on Poland disputes.

text.p: Warsaw and the EU have not solved their row over duty-free imports of car parts for assembly in Poland by Korean carmaker Daewoo but they have made progress, European Trade Commissioner Leon Brittan said on Friday.

"We had a good discussion on the Daewoo case and I think there is an understanding of what is needed to resolve it, although it is quite complicated and has not yet been resolved," Brittan told a news conference after two days of talks in Warsaw.
Poland aims to begin talks on joining the European Union early next year, once the bloc's 15 members finish their inter-governmental conference.

Relations are complicated by some disputes, notably over a deal by which Poland has allowed Daewoo to import tens of thousands of car kits duty-free annually for easy assembly as part of its purchase last year of the FSO car plant in Warsaw.

EU manufacturers say this gives a major Asian rival a back-door entry into Europe and breaches the spirit of Poland's association agreement with the union. Poland, eager to attract investment from beyond Europe, has disputed this.
Polish Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati said experts were now in talks to find a mutually acceptable solution and hinted that Poland's contract with Daewoo may be at fault.

"I do not hide that this is a difficult matter and it could stem from the fact that in the past there were inadequate efforts during the negotiation of the contract with Daewoo," he told the same joint news conference.
Brittan met Poland's president and prime minister during his trip but did not hold formal negotiations -- which were however conducted by an EU team during his visit.
Rosati said an agreement was close in another dispute, over obligatory certification of EU goods in Poland.

Brittan said there were quite good prospects for settling the issue of Warsaw's bid to extend protection of its steel and oil sectors -- which led to tensions between the two last year and the drafting of a compromise deal.

Brittan, a strong advocate of Poland's EU membership, said all these matters were issues that could and would be resolved rather than obstacles to its entry, and urged Poland to continue economic reforms essential to its admission.

He said he believed the EU's Inter-Governmental Conference would end and Poland's entry talks would begin on time, adding that he had assured Polish leaders: "That process will not be subject to any artificial delays."
